replace.find:
A knock came from below. Sharp, impatient.

She found Aurelio Mascarenhas on the step with his straw boater in his hands and his brass telescope under his arm. The Goan photographer had his studio on the floor above the tailor on Hurumzi, with a balcony that looked straight at the harbour. He had photographed Zuhura once for a merchant's wife who wanted a picture of the woman who made her caps. He had been courteous and nosy in equal measure, asking after her mother, her prices, her brother's flute playing which he could hear from his balcony on quiet nights.

"Bi Zuhura." He bowed a little. His white moustache lifted with his smile. His fingers were yellow with chemicals and his linen suit looked as if he had slept in it. "Forgive the hour. I have a plate for you. And I thought you would want news."

She let him in. He set the telescope carefully by the wall and took the stool Bi Mwana had used. He smelled of collodion and lime soap.

"The plate can wait," she said. "Have you seen my brother?"

"Half of Stone Town's brothers are at the palace." Aurelio removed his pince-nez and polished it on his sleeve. His eyes without the glass looked tired and kind. "I photographed the gate this morning. Before they closed it. I have every guard's face on glass, which the English officers find very interesting, and the palace guards find very annoying. Your Khamis was not there then. But the town talks. Three rupees and rice, they say."

Zuhura's hands went cold. She busied them with pouring tea, dark and sweet with too much sugar because sugar covered shaking.

"He went," she said quietly. "At noon. I told him the pay story. I did not think he would run."

Aurelio watched her over the rim of the glass. He drank and set it down with a small click.

"Young men run toward drums. Old men run toward cameras." He smiled, then let the smile go. "Listen. The consul has sent word to Khalid. I heard it from a clerk who drinks my brandy. Leave the palace. The English have another sultan ready. If Khalid refuses, there will be guns."

"Those three little ships?" Zuhura said. "Khamis laughed at them."

"Today there are three." Aurelio fitted the pince-nez back on his nose. "Tomorrow there may be more. The big ones come fast when London whistles. You have time, Bi Zuhura. A day. Perhaps two. Get him out before the paper runs out."

She stared at him. The lamp hissed. Moths beat against the glass chimney.

"How? The gates are closed."

"Gates open for some things. Food. Caps for new guards." He nodded at her basket. "And the gate guard Juma owes you for three caps he has not paid for. Men remember debts when a woman stands in front of them."

Hope rose so sharp it hurt her teeth. She pressed her lips together.

"You know a great deal, Bwana Aurelio."

"I photograph a great deal." He stood and picked up his telescope. At the door he paused. "When you go, take only what you can carry in one basket. And do not go at noon when the officers watch. Go early, when men are sleepy and hungry."

After he left she sat a long time with the tea cooling. The lighthouse beam began its slow sweep, white across the rooftops, white across her wall. Somewhere near the palace someone played a flute, badly, and stopped.
She got up and took the covered pot of rice off the stove.

Near dawn the drums stopped all at once, and in the sudden quiet she heard the sea against the sea wall and the far clink of a rifle dropped on stone, and she knew with a certainty that sat like a coin on her tongue that tomorrow she would walk to those gates with a basket of white caps on her arm and lie to get inside, and that whether she found him proud or frightened would decide everything that came after.

She pulled her shawl close and went out into the alley toward Hurumzi Street, where Aurelio Mascarenhas, the Goan photographer, kept a studio above the tailor's with a balcony that looked straight at the harbour. He had photographed her once, for a merchant's wife who wanted a picture of the woman who made her caps, and had asked after her mother, her prices and her brother's flute playing, which he could hear from his balcony on quiet nights. He photographed officers. He photographed guards. If anyone in Stone Town knew how a sister got through a closed gate, it was the man who had every face on that gate on glass.
